hints: Focus on what actually decides electron number, the proton number and the charge, not the mass number on top.
Check pair 1 first. Both are neutral Cl atoms with proton number 17, so they both have 17 electrons despite different masses.
Now count electrons for the ions by adding for negative and subtracting for positive charge, then see which pairs both reach 18.
walkthrough:
**Recall the electron counting rule**

For any species, electrons = proton number (atomic number) minus charge. A negative charge adds electrons, a positive charge removes them.

$$\text{electrons} = Z - \text{charge}$$

**Check pair 1: $^{35}\text{Cl}$ and $^{37}\text{Cl}$**

Both are neutral chlorine atoms, so $Z = 17$. Mass numbers 35 and 37 only change neutrons, not electrons.

$$17 - 0 = 17 \text{ electrons each, so pair 1 matches}$$

**Check pair 2: $^{35}\text{Cl}^-$ and $^{40}\text{Ar}$**

Chloride ion gains one electron, argon is neutral with $Z = 18$.

$$\text{Cl}^-: 17 - (-1) = 18, \quad \text{Ar}: 18 - 0 = 18$$
So pair 2 matches, they are isoelectronic.

**Check pair 3: $^{40}\text{Ar}$ and $^{40}\text{K}^+$**

Potassium has $Z = 19$ but loses one electron as $\text{K}^+$.

$$\text{Ar}: 18, \quad \text{K}^+: 19 - (+1) = 18$$
So pair 3 also matches. All three pairs match.

options.A: Correct, because 1, 2 and 3 are all true. Pair 1 has 17 and 17, pairs 2 and 3 both have 18 and 18. All are isoelectronic pairs.
options.B: Incorrect. This option includes only 1 and 2. It wrongly leaves out pair 3, forgetting that $\text{K}^+$ loses one electron from 19 to give 18, the same as Ar.
options.C: Incorrect. This option includes only 2 and 3. It wrongly leaves out pair 1, thinking different mass numbers mean different electrons, but isotopes differ only in neutrons.
options.D: Incorrect. This option includes only 1. It misses the isoelectronic idea that $\text{Cl}^-$, Ar and $\text{K}^+$ all have the noble gas configuration of 18 electrons.
